summary:
The Altai Republic stands under the national framework of Russia, and no sub-national deviation from that framework has been identified in the sources; the territory is therefore assessed at the national score. For a visitor, Russia's laws apply in full within the republic: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, gender-marker changes on official documents are prohibited, same-sex marriage is banned, and the expanded propaganda statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, justifies gender transition.

Penalties under that statute reach administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as extremist, participation in the designated movement carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising it 6 to 10 years under Article 282.2. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention and deportation, and official national government warnings state this expressly to LGBT travellers.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, do not travel, for all travellers regardless of personal characteristic, citing wrongful detention, active war and arbitrary law enforcement. The advisory carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the designated international LGBT movement or for displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, while 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Because any police, hotel or transport identity check can set a visitor's documents against their presentation, and because gender-marker changes remain prohibited, document screening is the principal everyday exposure point in the territory. Enforcement volume is rising alongside severity: cases under the propaganda statutes have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia (SOGI, June 2025) records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, with the state able but not willing to provide protection. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown has been documented: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is separately documented. In July 2024 BBC Russian followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. Comparable coercion has been reported in the North Caucasus, where the UK Home Office note treats Chechnya as a distinct protection concern within the same national framework.
localsOnly:
Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. Residents of the Altai Republic are subject to the same 2013 propaganda law and its 2023 expansion, and to Article 282.2 following the Supreme Court's extremist designation.

Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions since the designation, the overwhelming majority administrative, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. At least 20 people faced criminal charges between January 2024 and June 2025, with the most severe exposures reaching 12 years' imprisonment for publishing-house staff charged in May 2025.

The state is assessed as able but not willing to provide protection against discriminatory treatment of openly LGBT+ people, and the UK Home Office treats LGBT+ Russians, including those in Chechnya, as a particular social group for refugee-convention purposes.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement action, raids, detentions or prosecutions specific to the Altai Republic; the territory's assessment rests on the national framework and on the absence of any identified regional deviation. Whether local police or courts apply the extremism and propaganda statutes at the national rate in this republic is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory contains no information on the availability of legal representation, medical care or safe accommodation for transgender visitors within the Altai Republic, and no territory-specific reporting on hate-motivated violence. The eighteenfold growth in propaganda cases and the 60 million ruble fine total are national figures with no regional breakdown provided.

The status of consular assistance for detained transgender foreigners in the territory is not sourced. Whether the Level 4 advisory's wrongful-detention warning has produced documented cases involving LGBT travellers in this republic remains unresolved.
